Otakar Šín was a Czechoslovakian Czechoslovak army officer who played a prominent role in the Czechoslovak resistance during World War II. He was born on July 7, 1911 in Dvorák's, Bohemia, Austria-Hungary (now in the Czech Republic) and died on May 7, 1952 in Czechoslovakia.

Šín joined the Czechoslovak army in 1934 and became an officer. During the German occupation of Czechoslovakia in World War II, he joined the resistance movement and became a key figure in the underground anti-Nazi organization PVO (Pomocná vojenská organizace), also known as the "Czechoslovak Military Organization."

In 1941, Šín was named the commander of the Prague uprising against the Nazi occupation. He led the resistance fighters in fierce battles against the German forces in the streets of Prague in May 1945 and played a crucial role in the liberation of the city.

After the war, Šín continued to serve in the Czechoslovak army and was promoted to the rank of general. However, in 1951 he was arrested by the Communist regime on charges of espionage and sabotage and was sentenced to death. He was executed by hanging on May 7, 1952, at the age of 40.

Otakar Šín is remembered as a hero of the Czechoslovak resistance during World War II and a symbol of the struggle for freedom and democracy. Streets and squares in the Czech Republic have been named in his honor, and his legacy lives on in the memory of the Czech people.
